notes.meaning: The people of Israel gathered from the farthest north in Dan to the southern border in Beersheba, together with the tribes living east of the Jordan in Gilead. They came together as one unified body before the Lord at Mizpah to deal with the shocking crime in Gibeah. Mizpah was a well-known meeting place in central Israel where the nation could assemble before God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that two different historical accounts were blended together here, since one tradition sets the assembly at Mizpah and another at Bethel.

notes.meaning: The leaders of all the tribes took their places at the front of this holy gathering of God's people. They stood like cornerstones holding the nation together in a time of crisis. In total, 400,000 armed foot soldiers assembled to carry out what needed to be done.

The tribe of Benjamin heard that the rest of the nation had gathered at Mizpah, but they chose to stay away in stubborn defiance. The leaders of Israel then opened the formal inquiry, asking for the full story of how this terrible evil occurred. Gibeah was only a few miles away, so Benjamin had every opportunity to come and answer for what happened.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that the first part of this verse belongs before verse 14 because it seems to break the flow of the inquiry at Mizpah.

notes.meaning: The Levite stepped forward as the husband of the murdered woman to give his testimony. He made sure to specify that the crime took place in Gibeah of Benjamin. He did this so no one would mistakenly blame another town named Gibeah in Judah.

The Levite stated that the men of Gibeah surrounded the house at night with evil intent. He claimed they planned to kill him, but instead they attacked and abused his concubine until she died. While his report described real violence, he carefully left out his own shameful choice to push her outside to save himself.

The Levite explained that he cut her body into pieces and sent them across the land to awaken the nation's conscience. He declared that the men had committed an outrageous, shameful act that violated God's holy standards. A crime of this magnitude could not be ignored by God's people.

The Levite urged the entire assembly to give their counsel and hand down a verdict. Because they were all children of Israel bound to God by covenant, they were responsible to punish such wickedness. He asked them to decide right then and there what steps must be taken.

The entire assembly rose up together with one heart and mind. They vowed that not a single man would return home or sleep in his own tent until this evil was dealt with. They were completely united in demanding justice.

The leaders laid out their battle plan against the guilty city of Gibeah. They decided to cast lots to determine how they would organize the attack and divide the duties. This ensured fairness and order as they prepared for war.

Israel drafted one-tenth of their forces—40,000 men out of the 400,000—to gather food and supplies for the camp. The remaining 360,000 soldiers could then focus entirely on the siege without running out of provisions. They prepared carefully, knowing that bringing Gibeah to justice might take time.

The armies of Israel gathered outside Gibeah, completely bound together in purpose. They stood united as comrades ready to see justice carried out. True unity among God's people was meant to defend what is right and holy.

Before attacking, Israel sent messengers to all the family clans of Benjamin to confront them about the outrage. They asked how such terrible wickedness could happen in their territory. This gave Benjamin an opportunity to do what was right and avoid a war between brothers.

Israel demanded that Benjamin hand over the guilty men of Gibeah so they could be executed to remove the evil from the nation. Instead of obeying God's law, Benjamin chose stubborn pride and family loyalty over justice. By shielding the criminals, the entire tribe shared in their guilt.

The Benjamites left their towns and gathered at Gibeah to defend it against the other tribes. Rather than turning over the murderers, they chose to take up weapons against their own brothers. What began as a local crime now exploded into a full-scale civil war.

Benjamin mobilized 26,000 swordsmen from their towns, in addition to 700 select warriors living in Gibeah. Though heavily outnumbered by the other tribes, they were confident in their strength and military skill. They assembled inside and around Gibeah to make their stand.

Among Benjamin's troops were 700 elite left-handed slingers who could strike a hair's breadth without missing. Using a leather sling allowed them to shoot stones from a safe distance with deadly power. This special unit gave Benjamin a major tactical advantage in battle.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic translations, following the Latin Vulgate, understand these warriors as being able to fight with both the left hand and the right hand with equal skill, rather than being strictly left-handed.

notes.meaning: The rest of the tribes of Israel numbered 400,000 trained and experienced swordsmen. They had vastly superior numbers compared to the smaller army of Benjamin. Every soldier was an experienced fighter ready to defend the covenant.

The Israelites traveled to Bethel to ask God which tribe should take the lead in attacking Benjamin. The Lord answered that Judah should go first, just as Judah had led the march in the wilderness and the conquests in Canaan. Israel asked who should lead rather than whether they should go, assuming that victory was guaranteed because their cause was right.

The Israelite army woke early the next morning and marched toward Gibeah to set up their camp. Judah led the way just as the Lord had directed. They took up positions to begin the assault against the guilty town.

The men of Israel marched out from their camp and formed their battle lines facing Gibeah. They prepared to fight both the local defenders and the Benjamite reinforcements. The stage was now set for a fierce clash between brother tribes.

The Benjamite forces charged out from Gibeah and slaughtered 22,000 Israelite soldiers that day. Israel had trusted in its enormous army and its good cause, but God had not promised them immediate victory. This shocking defeat humbled the nation and taught them not to rely on their own strength.

Despite the terrible loss, the Israelite soldiers encouraged one another and rallied their forces. They took up the exact same battle positions they had occupied on the first day. They remained determined to carry out justice and refused to back down in fear.

The Israelites went up to Bethel and wept before the Lord until evening, deeply shaken by the loss of their men. They asked God whether they should go out to fight against their brother Benjamin again, and the Lord told them to go up. Their tears showed real sorrow over the cost of the conflict and a growing humility before God.

On the second day of fighting, the army of Israel advanced once more against the Benjamites. They obeyed the Lord's instruction to go forward even after suffering heavy heartbreak. Standing for what is right often requires great endurance through deep pain.
